body:
Steps are no longer ordered by train and date. Each new step is weighed against every open one and the whole queue is ranked again: repairs first, then the steps others wait on, then bugs before features, with date used only to break a tie. Each place comes with one line saying why. Two steps that touch the same files never run at the same time, and a launch out of order is refused with the step that should go first named. One limit: a step's wording rarely proves it repairs lost data, so the orchestrator says so when it plans the step, and the step then goes to the top.

### How a pair is measured (scripts/kit.py, the R6 section before `step_new`)
For each pair of open train steps, from facts:
- **Repair:** the post's `damage` field (set with `step new --damage`), or damage wording in the title and the task's first two sentences ("overwrote", "posts lost", "wiped"...). A negation such as "never overwrites" is not damage, and history further down the task does not count.
- **Waits on:** `after`/`blocked_by`, or the task saying so with a cue: "waits on M1", "after CL51", "builds on M3", "once CL47 lands". A bare mention such as "CL44's part did X" is history, not a wait. A task that says every step waits behind it (CL47) counts as unblocking all of them.
- **Same files / same area:** the files a step's pieces name, plus the paths in its task, compared by name (kit.py, .kit/kit.py and scripts/kit.py are one file). Areas come from M1's `map.areas` globs when present.
- **A bug in what the other builds:** a bug and a feature on the same files: the bug goes first.

### The order and what runs together
Steps are ordered so that no step comes before one it waits on. Among the steps that are ready, the order is: repair, then the most steps waiting on it (directly or not), then bug, then oldest. Going down the queue, a step can start when it waits on nothing open and shares no file or area with a running step or with a step above it that can start. Otherwise it shows `waits: CL16 first (...)` or `CL44 runs (shares install.py)`.

### Where it shows
- `kit.py queue` (no `--runner`/`--for`): the ranked steps, one line each, then the cards as before. With `--runner`/`--for` it works as before (the MCP `board_queue` is unchanged).
- The orchestrator's resume: a "The queue" section, the first 12 lines.
- `step new`: its answer carries the re-ranked `queue`, and `pause` for each running step a repair would undo (with its session id and the message to send).
- `kit.py launch`: refused when out of order (`out of order: D1 goes first (place 1, F1 is 2): ...; launch \`d\``); `--anyway "<why>"` launches it and records the reason. A relaunch or a takeover is not checked again.
- The orchestrator guides (kit/orchestrator.template.md, kit/claude-cli/orchestrator.template.md and their .kit copies) replace "launch several at once when they do not touch the same files" with the queue rule.

### One choice I made: a file most steps name
kit.py is named by most open steps (more than half, with at least 4 steps). Counting it as a clash would let only one step run at a time. As in the split check (0eca719: different functions of one big file merge cleanly), such a file alone is not a clash, and the queue says so on its last line. `"kit": {"queue": {"strict_files": true}}` in .kit/config.json counts it too, if you want it literal.

### Tests
tests/test_queue_rank.py (fixture board, nothing real read or written): the six cases in the bars. The full run: 71 passed, 0 failed. tests/test_resume_attached_boards.py's byte-for-byte control now leaves out the new queue section, as it already did for CL28's. Its agy test failed once in a first run here and on the base commit too (78df8a0, before this step); it passed in the full run.

When CL51 and R6 land, git merges them; then push those two files to the board again. `kit.queue_rank(posts)` returns each open step's place, why, can_start and waits. `order_problem(posts, pid)` is the launch check and `pause_messages(posts, pid)` gives the running steps a repair would undo. `step new` takes `--damage "<what was lost, who found it>"`, `--after <PART>` and `--kind bug|feature`, and its answer carries `queue` and `pause`. `launch --anyway "<why>"` writes `launched_out_of_order` on the post. When M1's map lands on the trunk, `map.areas` globs in .kit/config.json make an area clash like a file.

task:
Every new step is measured against every open step, for its place in the queue and for what can run beside it; the queue is re-ranked at each new step, never ordered by date. Today the kit sorts steps by train, then by date (scripts/kit.py); the priority the workstreams had on 11-20 (P1-P3, sorted) was lost on 11-22 when the train became the task list (2e74fce), and nobody noticed. On 2026-11-26 the web orchestrator launched M5 to M8 (features) while CL51 waited; CL51's bug then overwrote 11 posts. Concurrency is not measured between steps either: the split check (0eca719) looks inside one step only; between steps the guide just says "launch several at once when they do not touch the same files".

1. At `step new` (and at each resume while steps are open) the new step is compared with each open one, pair by pair, on facts: does it repair damage (data lost or wrong, found by a review, a done or the owner) or put data at risk; does the other wait on it (it changes what the other builds on, or the other would redo or undo its work); do they touch the same files or the same area of the map (M1); is one a bug in what the other builds. In scripts/kit.py.
2. From those pairs: the queue order (damage first; then what unblocks the most steps; then bugs before features; date only to break a tie), and the running sets: two steps that share files or an area never run at the same time; the later one waits, named.
3. Every new step re-ranks the whole queue; resume and `kit.py queue` show it with one line of why for each place ("before M2: M2 builds on the format this fixes"); the orchestrator launches from its top, and a launch out of order is refused with the step that should go first named (`--anyway "<why>"` records it).
4. A step already running that a new P1 step would undo or redo gets a message to pause at its next save point.
5. Tests on a fixture board: a new damage step goes to the top; a step that two others wait on goes before them; two steps on the same file never both run; a launch out of order is refused.
title: Every new step is measured against every open one: queue order and what runs together
verdict: Yes: the queue is re-ranked at every new step and every resume, a reason on each line; same-file steps never run together; an out-of-order launch is refused, naming the step to launch first.
